title: Doctor App Development: Roster, Queue, e-Prescription
meta: Doctor app development for hospitals and clinics: today's roster, the live consult queue, EMR on rounds, e-prescription and imaging opened from an AuraPACS link.
h1: Doctor app development for the consultant who is never at a desk.
sub: A doctor app puts the roster, the consult queue, the patient's record, e-prescription and imaging on the consultant's phone. We build it on HIMS and AuraPACS so nothing is retyped and every action lands in the hospital record.
meta_ticks: Imaging opened from an AuraPACS link
whatsapp_text: Hi, I'd like to discuss a doctor app for our hospital or clinic.
persona: Medical director, hospital IT head or polyclinic owner who wants doctors working from a phone

paras: Doctor app development produces a mobile app for the consultants of a hospital or clinic. It shows each doctor's roster, the consult queue for the current session, the patient's EMR when a token is called, and lets the doctor write an e-prescription, order investigations and open imaging, all against the encounter in the hospital system.

Elevate Aura builds the doctor app on HIMS, where doctor rosters, the OP queue, EMR, e-prescription, pharmacy and laboratory already exist as modules, and on AuraPACS for imaging, which opens in a browser viewer from a link with no download. The app is for Android and iOS from one codebase.
The result is a consultant who can run a session, do rounds and answer a report query from a phone, while the hospital record stays complete.

sections.h2: Why doctors end up on WhatsApp instead of the hospital system.
sections.lead: Desktop systems assume the doctor is sitting in front of them. Most of a consultant's day happens somewhere else.

items.p: Session times and room changes arrive as texts from the coordinator, and the doctor arrives to a queue nobody told them about.
Handwritten scripts are retyped at the pharmacy, or not typed at all, so the EMR is missing the one thing that matters.
A junior sends a photo of the X-ray to the consultant's phone. The read is done on a compressed image with no window and level.
On the ward the doctor asks the nurse for last night's vitals because the system is at the station, not at the bed.
The consultant does not know how many patients are waiting, so sessions overrun and walk-ins are turned away.

items.q: Does the doctor app replace the HIMS desktop?
items.a: No. It is a mobile front on the same modules. Detailed documentation, discharge summaries and billing stay on the desktop where a keyboard helps. The app covers what a doctor does while moving: roster, queue, consult, prescription and reports.

items.q: How does the doctor view scans?
items.a: Each study in AuraPACS has a link that opens the zero-download browser viewer. From the app the doctor opens CT, MR, X-ray or ultrasound with slice scrolling and window/level on a phone or laptop. The diagnostic read remains with the hospital's radiologist.

items.q: Can doctors write prescriptions in the app?
items.a: Yes. E-prescription is a HIMS module. The prescription is saved against the encounter and appears in the pharmacy dispensing queue, so the pharmacy does not retype it from paper.

items.q: Can one doctor use it across two hospitals?
items.a: If both hospitals run HIMS the roster can show sessions per site. Across different systems each site needs its own connection, which we discuss on the call.

items.q: Does it need a strong network?
items.a: The queue and EMR need a connection to stay live, but notes and prescriptions drafted on a weak ward connection are held on the device and saved when it returns.
Each doctor sees only their own sessions and the patients under their care, with role-based access and an audit log in HIMS. Access is revoked centrally when a doctor leaves.
